## Aside: Hiding code chunks

Unless you're communicating to a technical audience that is specifically interested in seeing your code, you should consider using Quarto's chunk options to hide the low-level details of your analysis.
The `#| echo: false` option will disable showing code in the output.
Check the `eda.qmd` source on GitHub to see how we load the packages and data.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

penguins = pd.read_csv("penguins.csv").dropna()
```

## Checking for balance across groups

```{python}
#| echo: false
penguins.groupby(["species", "sex"]).agg(
  n = ("species", "count")
)
```

The Adelie and Chinstrap groups are perfectly balanced, even after dropping entries with missing values.
This will be an advantage for any hypothesis tests and suggests some control over confounding.
However, keep in mind we are not looking at `island`; we saw before that it can be used as a proxy for `species`.

## Some descriptive statistics

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: "center"
#| label: fig-bodymass
#| fig-cap: "Average body mass by species and sex."
fig = sns.catplot(
  data = penguins,
  kind = "bar",
  x = "species",
  y = "body_mass_g",
  hue = "sex",
  errorbar = None,
)

fig.despine(left = True)
fig.set_axis_labels("", "Body mass (g)")
fig.legend.set_title("")

fig
```


```{python}
#| echo: false
agg_dict = {
  "n": ("species", "count"),
  "Body Mass (g)": ("body_mass_g", "mean"),
}

(
  penguins
  .groupby("species")
  .agg(**agg_dict)
  .round(2)
  .reset_index()
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
(
  penguins
  .groupby("sex")
  .agg(**agg_dict)
  .round(2)
  .reset_index()
)
```

Treated separately, we can see that male penguins have a higher body mass across each species (@fig-bodymass)
When combined, the female penguins bring down the average body mass for each species.
We can see this effect by examining average body mass by sex or species alone.
